title: How Much Is One Recurrence Worth? Iso-Depth Scaling Laws for Looped Language Models
relevance_reason: Joint scaling law that measures the worth of one recurrence in unique parameters under matched effective depth and training FLOPs.
one_sentence: 116-run iso-depth (20 effective layers) sweep over r in {1,2,4,8} fits L = E + A(N_once + r^phi N_rec)^-alpha + B D^-beta, finding phi = 0.46: a recurrence is worth about half a unique block, so looping loses at matched compute.
key_contributions: Recurrence-equivalence exponent phi in a joint Chinchilla-style law; phi = 0.46 (95% CI [0.41, 0.53]) on a prelude-2/recur/coda-2 baseline with linear injection and full BPTT.
Delta-phi as a diagnostic: truncated BPTT lowers loss but drops phi to 0.38 (loop mechanism undertrained, wider optimum, higher inference cost); loop-boundary hyperconnections raise phi to 0.65.

Downstream five-axis suite: parametric knowledge tracks the capacity loss of looping, reasoning axes show no above-noise looped advantage at these budgets; gap persists at a ~4e20 FLOP, 47B-token extrapolation run.

claims.evidence_quote: Our φ = 0.46 sits in between, so replacing unique blocks with shared recurrences increases validation loss at matched training compute.

claims.claim: The compute-optimal loss gap of looped vs non-looped grows with r and persists at ~20x the grid compute (0.061 nats at r=4, 47B tokens).
claims.regime: iso_data; iso_effective_depth (matched tokens, looped has ~3% FLOP advantage)
claims.evidence_quote: The looped model trails by 0.061 nats in validation loss, inside the [0.05, 0.08] nats r=4 band measured across the grid.

claims.claim: Truncated BPTT (backprop through last ceil(r/2) loops) lowers validation loss via more tokens but lowers phi to 0.38, i.e. the loop mechanism is trained worse and the optimum shifts to wider, costlier models.
claims.evidence_quote: However, the measured φ disagrees, dropping from 0.45 to 0.38 (Table 3). So each additional recurrence is now worth much less in unique-parameter terms than before

claims.claim: Hyperconnections at the loop boundary raise phi to 0.65 and move the compute optimum to narrower widths (a genuine capacity gain); r=2 matches or beats r=1 at some budgets.
claims.evidence_quote: hyperconnections substantially lower validation loss across all looped runs, and φ jumps from 0.45 to 0.65 (Table 3).

claims.claim: Downstream, parametric-knowledge tasks track the looped models' capacity loss while reasoning-heavy axes show no above-noise looped advantage, even at the extrapolation run.
claims.evidence_quote: Parametric-knowledge tasks track validation loss directly, while reasoning-heavy tasks on which looped models are predicted to excel show no above-noise architectural signal at our budgets, not even at the ∼20× extrapolation runs.

claims.claim: Literature synthesis: in trained looped LMs effective inference depth concentrates near the training depth distribution rather than extrapolating past it, so r is treated as an architectural rather than test-time axis.
claims.evidence_quote: Taken together, effective inference depth in trained looped LMs concentrates near the training depth distribution rather than extrapolating freely past it.

survey_notes: Cleanest controlled evidence that looping costs quality at matched training FLOPs and matched effective depth (phi=0.46 < 1). Directly complements Parcae (2604.12946), which fixes unique parameters and lets depth/FLOPs/KV grow (iso-param): the two laws answer different questions and are not contradictory. Truncated BPTT result is a warning for Huginn/Parcae/retrofit recipes that use it.

title: Scaling Laws for Looped Mixture of Experts
relevance_reason: Joint scaling law over model size, data, recurrence and MoE sparsity for middle-block looped (MoE) transformers, with a compute-matched trillion-token validation.
one_sentence: Fits a Chinchilla/MoE-style law with a bounded, sparsity-conditional effective-parameter mapping N_eff = N_act + kappa1(m) N_loop (1 - e^{-(R-1)/kappa2(m)}); recurrence gains saturate, sparsity raises the ceiling; a 1.3B-total looped MoE matches a 2.9B MoE on reasoning at matched training FLOPs.
key_contributions: Bounded recurrence mapping (finite asymptote kappa1 N_loop) that beats linear (Parcae-style) and power-law (Iso-Depth-style) mappings on held-out R=16, N and D; sparsity-conditional kappa_j(m) = kappa_j m^-theta.
Fitted law used for compute-optimal R* (grows with compute and sparsity, larger for smaller models) and memory-optimal expert count; tight memory favors recurrence, more memory favors sparsity.

Downstream (14 benchmarks): sparsity gives ~3x active-parameter efficiency overall, recurrence ~2x total-parameter efficiency on reasoning (BBH, GSM8K) at matched training FLOPs; ~3T-token LoopMoE (R=5) vs ~6T-token 2x larger MoE at ~1.5e22 FLOPs.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: sweep D in {100,...,500}B tokens of an open-licensed web-heavy mix; LoopMoE ~3T tokens vs MoE ~6T tokens (~1.5e22 FLOPs each)
setup.loops_train: R in {1,2,3,4,6,8} (R=16 held out); middle block looped with 2 prelude and 2 coda layers; LoopMoE R*=5 with per-loop supervision

setup.benchmarks: BBH, GSM8K, ARC-C/E, OpenBookQA, HellaSwag, PIQA, SIQA, WinoGrande, BoolQ, DROP, MMLU, Natural Questions, TriviaQA

claims.claim: Recurrence adds effective parameters only up to a finite asymptote; MoE sparsity raises that asymptote and delays saturation (routing reaches different experts across passes).
claims.regime: iso_param; iso_data (fixed N_act and D in the sweep)
claims.evidence_quote: Finding: Scaling recurrence adds effective-parameter gain up to a finite, sparsity-dependent asymptote, while scaling sparsity raises and sustains this gain over more recurrent passes.

claims.claim: The bounded mapping extrapolates better to unseen R=16 than linear (overestimates) and power-law (overly optimistic) mappings used by prior looped scaling laws.
claims.evidence_quote: The linear mapping substantially overestimates the effective-parameter gain, while the power-law mapping captures diminishing gains but remains overly optimistic beyond the fitted range.

claims.claim: At matched training FLOPs (E=8), more recurrence lets a smaller model match a model with about 2x the total parameters on reasoning (GSM8K, BBH).
claims.evidence_quote: These recurrence gains can offset a ∼2× increase in total parameters on Reasoning: at 1021 FLOPs, the 0.3B model with R≥4 matches or exceeds the 0.6B model with R=1, while the 0.6B model with R≥3 matches the 1.0B model with R=1.

claims.claim: Compute-optimal recurrence grows with training budget and sparsity; under fixed compute, tight weight-memory budgets favor recurrence and large budgets favor sparsity.
claims.evidence_quote: Finding: At fixed compute, tight memory favors recurrence, and more memory favors sparsity.

limitations: Only middle-block looping studied; law asymptotes are properties within the observed R range (R<=8 fitted, R=16 held out); weight memory only (KV cache excluded); trillion-token LoopMoE trails the 2x MoE on overall score and needs up to 1.8x its inference compute; sweep models use last-pass loss only.
survey_notes: Third family of looped scaling laws: bounded (saturating) mapping vs Parcae's linear unrolled-parameter mapping and Iso-Depth's power law; argues both prior mappings are unbounded and over-predict at large R. Dense fitted asymptote kappa1 = 0.3682 (times N_loop), i.e. dense looping is worth little in the limit, consistent in direction with Iso-Depth phi=0.46 and with Sparse Layers (2605.09165) that dense looping scales poorly while Looped-MoE scales well. Positive downstream claims are iso_train_flop at fixed sparsity but the looped model uses more inference FLOPs (up to 1.8x) and fewer tokens; the reasoning-vs-overall split (matches 2x MoE on BBH/GSM8K, trails overall) supports the 'loops help reasoning more than knowledge' pattern (Ouro, Iso-Depth parametric-knowledge axis). Law-derived recurrence R*=5 contrasts with SMELT's choice of looping twice and LoopCoder-v2's saturation at 2 loops; different matching rules (SMELT matches total params and per-token FLOPs too).

title: SMELT: Scaling Laws for Compute-Matched MoE Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Multi-scale (to 54B total params) MoE looped Transformer study matching per-token FLOPs, total parameters and KV cache, with separate Chinchilla-style fits per architecture.
one_sentence: Loops the middle half of an MoE Transformer twice while matching per-token FLOPs, total parameters and KV cache (narrower width, more experts, smaller heads); across 100M-1.6B active (to 54B total) it saves 6.8-18.0% training FLOPs on the frontier.
key_contributions: Budget-matched recipe: loop middle 50% of layers twice, narrow hidden size, raise expert count to recover total params, adjust head size/GQA to hold KV cache, scale looped residual updates by 1/r.
4 scales x 4 sparsity grid (96 matched pairs, up to ~215B tokens) with separate surfaces L(F,S,D) = E + A(1-S)^b/F^a + K/D^c; SMELT has steeper frontier exponent (0.250 vs 0.237).
Downstream gains exceed what validation loss predicts and grow with scale; gains largest on Code, long samples and with more in-context examples; second visit reduces attention sink.

limitations: Design ablations only at 200M active (3.9B total); each configuration trained once (no training-seed variance); only contiguous fully shared block looping; matching is on arithmetic FLOPs, params and KV size, not wall-clock; frontier gains at 1e22 are extrapolated; mechanism probes are descriptive.
survey_notes: Strongest controlled positive evidence for looping: matched per-token FLOPs (inference and training), total params, KV cache and identical data, up to 54B total params. Apparent contradiction with Iso-Depth (2604.21106, phi=0.46, looping loses at matched FLOPs): regime differs, since Iso-Depth holds width fixed and lets unique params shrink by up to 3.2x, whereas SMELT recovers total params via extra experts and narrows width; the authors explicitly argue Iso-Depth's deficit may reflect parameter loss. Also dense vs MoE: consistent with Sparse Layers (2605.09165) and Loop Scaling Laws (2609.40316) that sparsity rescues looping. Loop-count result (2 best under FLOP matching) agrees with LoopCoder-v2 (2606.18023, saturation at 2 loops, different mechanism) and with Gao et al. (cited, 2 loop steps optimal under wall-clock matching), but differs from Loop Scaling Laws' law-derived R*=5, which matches only training FLOPs and lets inference FLOPs grow. Gains on code and in-context learning are measured via loss and DCLM; no explicit reasoning benchmark like GSM8K at these scales.

title: Parcae: Scaling Laws For Stable Looped Language Models
relevance_reason: Stable prelude-recur-coda looped LM with iso-parameter isoFLOP training scaling laws over mean recurrence and a unified train/test-time recurrence law.
one_sentence: Recasts looping as a dynamical system, constrains injection spectral norm (negative diagonal A, ZOH) for stability, and derives iso-parameter scaling laws: compute-optimal training raises mean recurrence and data together; test-time looping saturates exponentially near training depth.
key_contributions: LTI analysis showing divergent looped runs learn rho(A) >= 1; Parcae parameterizes A = Diag(-exp(log A)) with ZOH discretization, normalizes the injected input, and samples depth per sequence.
Iso-parameter isoFLOP sweeps at 140M and 370M: optimal mu_rec ~ C^0.40 and tokens ~ C^0.78; looping frontier strictly below fixed-depth at matched params and FLOPs.

Test-time law L(T) = L_inf + Z exp(-zT) with L_inf equal to the training-law loss at T = mu_rec, unified as a training floor plus exp(-z T / mu_rec) decay; 1.3B/104B-token comparison with parameter- and data-matched Transformers.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: FineWeb-Edu; 11.2B/29.6B/61.6B/104B tokens for 140M/370M/770M/1.3B; isoFLOP budgets 1e18-6.4e19 (140M) and 3.2e19-1.28e20 (370M)

setup.baselines: parameter- and data-matched Transformers (nanochat) and RDMs (Huginn-style recurrent depth models); fixed-depth (mu_rec=1) Parcae at matched params and FLOPs
setup.benchmarks: validation PPL, WikiText, Lambada, Core and Core-Extended (DCLM suites), HellaSwag, ARC, PIQA, BoolQ, SciQ

claims.claim: Instability of prior looped models (residual explosion) is tied to learning an injection transition with spectral radius >= 1; constraining it yields convergence across learning rates where baselines diverge.
claims.evidence_quote: Figure 3 and Table 2 confirm this empirically: divergent runs learn a spectral radius of ρ(A) ≥ 1, with convergent runs maintaining ρ(A) < 1, affirming that LTI stability constraints are necessary.

claims.claim: At matched unique parameters and training tokens (but more FLOPs for Parcae, mu_rec=8 on the middle third), Parcae beats Transformers on validation PPL and Core/Core-Extended at all four scales up to 1.3B.
claims.evidence_quote: Table 5 shows that Parcae reduces validation perplexity by 4.3–9.2% and improves Core and Core-Extended Scores by up to 2.99 and 1.18 points, respectively.

claims.claim: At fixed parameter count and fixed training FLOPs, the compute-optimal looped frontier (fewer tokens, more recurrence) achieves strictly lower loss and higher Core than fixed-depth models that spend the FLOPs on more data.
claims.evidence_quote: Figure 6 shows fixed-depth Parcae models without looping at each FLOP budget. The optimal curve achieves a strictly lower loss, which translates to 1.2-2.0 points higher Core scores (Table 6).

claims.claim: Compute-optimal training increases mean recurrence and data in tandem following power laws.
claims.evidence_quote: Our initial scaling laws suggest that looping and data should be increased in tandem, given a fixed FLOP budget.

claims.claim: Test-time looping does not extrapolate past training depth in language modeling: gains plateau near the training mean recurrence and follow a saturating exponential.
claims.evidence_quote: we observe that gains plateau near µrec , suggesting training depth determines the test-time scaling ceiling.

claims.claim: Truncating the sampling distribution by the backprop depth hurts extrapolation to lower and higher recurrences, and deeper test-time recurrence quality is coupled to the backprop depth.
claims.evidence_quote: This implies that the capabilities of looped models utilizing deeper recurrences are heavily coupled with µbwd .

survey_notes: Key iso-parameter scaling-law paper. Its positive results hold at fixed unique parameters (iso_param) where looping adds FLOPs; at fixed params AND fixed FLOPs, looping beats spending compute on more data (iso_param + iso_train_flop), which is NOT the same question as Iso-Depth (2604.21106), which fixes effective depth and FLOPs and lets unique params vary and finds looping loses (phi=0.46). Both can be true: looping is a good use of extra FLOPs when parameters (memory) are capped, but a worse use than unique layers when they are not. Iso-Depth explicitly frames Parcae as complementary and notes Parcae uses truncated BPTT, which Iso-Depth finds lowers phi. Test-time result (saturation at mu_rec) agrees with Ouro (degradation beyond T=4) and contradicts strong extrapolation claims from synthetic tasks. The 'twice the size' claim compares a 770M looped model (8 middle-third loops, more FLOPs) to a 1.3B Transformer on the same data; FLOPs are not matched.

title: Nanbeige4.2-3B: Unlocking Agentic Capabilities in a Compact Model
relevance_reason: Open-weight 3B non-embedding looped Transformer (two passes over the full stack) pretrained from scratch on 28T tokens, then SFT and agentic RL.
one_sentence: Technical report of a 3B non-embedding two-pass looped Transformer pretrained on 28T tokens and post-trained for agents; reports wins over larger public models (Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma4-12B) on agentic benchmarks, with only qualitative loop ablations.
key_contributions: Largest-token-budget looped LM in the corpus: 28T tokens, whole-stack two-pass loop, released weights.

Qualitative design findings: from-scratch looping beats upcycling a pretrained dense model; two passes best (about 75% of standard-Transformer token efficiency); halving KV by sharing across passes costs performance.
Agentic SFT/RL pipeline (mixed-mode RLHF, length-controlled reasoning RL, agentic RL with process rewards) on top of the looped base.

title: LoopCoder-v2: Only Loop Once for Efficient Test-Time Computation Scaling
relevance_reason: 7B Parallel Loop Transformer coders trained from scratch on 18T tokens at R=1-4 with matched SFT; non-monotonic loop-count effect with per-loop diagnostics.
one_sentence: Trains 7B Parallel Loop Transformer coders at R=1,2,3,4 on the same 18T tokens and SFT; R=2 sharply improves code and agentic benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified 43.0 to 64.4) while R>=3 regresses, explained by a fixed cross-loop-offset cost versus shrinking per-loop gain.
key_contributions: Large matched loop-count study: four 7B PLT models from scratch on 18T tokens (1:1 text:code), identical 6M-example SFT, evaluated at their training loop count.

Gain-cost diagnosis: loop 2 carries the productive refinement (effective rank peaks, largest output shift); later loops oscillate, and the CLP positional-mismatch cost stays roughly fixed and exceeds per-loop gain by 30-45x.
Thinking (explicit CoT) on top of the R=2 latent loop is super-additive on reasoning benchmarks (e.g. +26.9 on LiveCodeBench).

title: Scaling Latent Reasoning via Looped Language Models
relevance_reason: Largest openly released from-scratch looped LM family (1.4B/2.6B, 7.7T tokens) with learned exit gate, synthetic knowledge-capacity/manipulation study and small-scale loop scaling laws.
one_sentence: Pretrains Ouro, weight-tied whole-stack LoopLMs (1.4B, 2.6B; 4 loops; 7.7T tokens) with an entropy-regularized exit gate; claims 2-3x parameter efficiency vs public dense checkpoints and attributes gains to knowledge manipulation, not storage.
key_contributions: Ouro-1.4B (24 layers x 4) and Ouro-2.6B (48 layers x 4, upcycled by layer duplication) trained on 7.7T tokens plus Thinking SFT variants, released openly.

Entropy-regularized (uniform-prior ELBO) exit-gate objective plus a Stage-II gate fine-tune using per-step loss improvement; Q-exit thresholding at inference; last-step KV reuse cuts decode KV memory 4x.

Capo/Mano/multi-hop-QA synthetic studies: looping leaves knowledge capacity at ~2 bits/param but improves knowledge manipulation; small-scale total-loss and step-wise-loss scaling laws (53M-1.36B, 20B tokens).

title: Sparse Layers are Critical to Scaling Looped Language Models
relevance_reason: Controlled isoFLOP scaling comparison of dense, MoE, looped and looped-MoE transformers at matched effective depth, plus early exit at loop boundaries.
one_sentence: IsoFLOP study (5e16-1e18 FLOPs, 16 effective layers) shows dense looping strictly hurts at matched compute, while replacing dense FFNs by top-2-of-8 MoE lets a looped model beat the dense baseline; loop boundaries are better training-free early-exit points.
key_contributions: Four architectures (Base, MoE, Looped 8x2, Looped-MoE 8x2) with identical active parameters and effective depth, compared with muP-transferred isoFLOP scaling laws.
Mechanism: expert routing diverges across loop passes (25-53% of tokens get fully disjoint experts in most layers), recovering per-pass expressivity.
Entropy-based early exit: looped models degrade less per FLOP saved because each loop ends with the output-facing layers; more loops (2x8) improve the trade-off further.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: FineWeb-Edu 10B-token sample, GPT-2 tokenizer; D = C/(6 N_active)
setup.loops_train: 8 layers x 2 loops (scaling study); 4x4 and 2x8 for early-exit study
setup.loops_test: same; early exit only at loop boundaries
setup.baselines: Base (16 unique dense layers) and non-looped MoE at the same active parameters and effective depth
setup.benchmarks: test loss; AI2 OLMES Core 9 (ARC-E/C, BoolQ, CSQA, HellaSwag, OBQA, PIQA, SIQA, WinoGrande); perplexity vs FLOPs saved

claims.claim: At matched training compute and effective depth, dense looping scales strictly worse than the dense baseline, while Looped-MoE scales better than the dense baseline.
claims.evidence_quote: We find that Looped-MoE scales better than Base, while Looped models scale strictly worse (Figure 1, middle), supporting our hypothesis that sparse routing restores expressiveness lost to weight tying.

claims.claim: Looping the same architecture always reduces quality at matched compute: non-looped MoE beats Looped-MoE and Base beats Looped; all four share roughly the same slope and differ in offset.
claims.evidence_quote: MoE scales the best, followed by Looped-MoE, then Base and lastly Looped. Looping the same architecture seems thus to strictly reduce expressivity.

claims.claim: Downstream at 1e18 FLOPs, Looped-MoE has the highest OLMES Core 9 average with fewer stored parameters than Base; dense Looped is lowest; non-looped MoE is lowest overall despite best test loss.
claims.evidence_quote: Looped-MoE achieves the highest average score (39.6) across the Core 9 benchmarks, outperforming Base (38.7) despite storing fewer unique parameters (216M vs. 246M). Looped scores lowest (37.4)

claims.claim: MoE routing diverges across loop passes, so the same physical layer runs different expert sub-networks on each pass.
claims.evidence_quote: Across layers 1–6 and 8, 25–53% of tokens receive entirely non-overlapping expert assignments between passes, while only 4–14% receive identical assignments.

claims.claim: Looped models give better training-free early-exit compute-quality trade-offs than non-looped models, and more loops improve this further.
claims.evidence_quote: at 10% FLOPs saved, Looped and Looped-MoE reach perplexity 50.2 and 51.0, compared to 55.4 for Base and 75.7 for MoE.

claims.claim: Critique of Ouro: Ouro compares by unique parameters while giving its models 4x the effective depth (more compute) than the dense models it is compared to.
claims.evidence_quote: In their study, they compare performance by the number of unique parameters, but giving their models much more compute (4x the effective depth) than the models in their comparisons.

title: Looped Language Models Improve Compositional Tool Calling

one_sentence: LoRA-SFTs Ouro-1.4B/2.6B, retrofitted looped Llama-3.2-1B/OLMo-2-1B and non-looped baselines on the same function-calling data; looped models gain most on multi-call and nested tool use, accuracy rises with inference depth, and Ouro's exit gate gives a better compute trade-off.
key_contributions: Matched-SFT comparison of looped vs non-looped models on BFCL v3, NESTful and API-Bank, separating compositional (multi-call, nested) from single-call tool use.
Inference-depth sweeps (Ouro 1-4, retrofits 1-8) showing gains concentrate on compositional categories and saturate (Ouro-2.6B near-saturated after 3 iterations).
Adaptive exit (Ouro gate, thresholds q) matches or slightly exceeds the best fixed depth on BFCL with fewer average iterations.

survey_notes: Capability evidence for compositional/agentic use of looped models, but regime is weak: Ouro vs Qwen3/Llama differ in pretraining, and the same-recipe SFT baselines underperform their own public instruct versions dramatically on multi-call tasks, while public Qwen3-1.7B/4B-Instruct exceed the SFT'd Ouro models on BFCL overall. The cleanest evidence is the within-model inference-depth sweep (depth helps compositional categories, saturating by 3-4 for Ouro-2.6B) and the adaptive-exit result. Consistent with Ouro's claim that loops help composition/manipulation more than retrieval, and with Nanbeige4.2/LoopCoder-v2 agentic claims, which are also unmatched or FLOP-unmatched. Retrofit vs native gap echoes Nanbeige4.2's statement that from-scratch looping beats upcycling.

title: Squeezing More from Limited Data with Recursive Transformers
relevance_reason: Whole-stack weight-shared causal LM (RecursiveGPT) as a compute-scaling axis under fixed 10M-100M word data budgets, compared with standard Transformers and FLOP-matched extra epochs.
one_sentence: Under fixed BabyLM-scale data (10M-100M words) where larger standard models overfit, a recursive decoder with per-step norms and factorized embeddings outperforms standard Transformers and FLOP-matched extra-epoch training.
key_contributions: Optimal-scale sweep of standard Transformers (13M-1.2B params, 10M-100M words, two corpora): optimum depends on data budget and downstream target; extra parameters overfit.
RecursiveGPT: one shared block applied R times with step-specific RMSNorm and biases, MLP expansion 16, factorized embeddings; depth sweep peaks at R=16.
Compute-matched control: spending the same FLOPs on more epochs (146 at 10M words, 50 at 100M) degrades the standard model, whereas recursion improves it.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: BabyLM baseline corpus and Nemotron-ClimbMix; 10M-100M words, 10 epochs
setup.baselines: standard 12-layer Transformers with/without factorized embeddings on the same data; standard models trained for more epochs to match FLOPs; BabyLM 2025 GPT-BERT and AMLM hard decay (unmatched recipes)
setup.benchmarks: BLiMP, COMPS, LAMBADA pass@5; BLiMP Supplement, EWoK, Entity Tracking

claims.claim: At a fixed 10M-word data budget, a 27.6M recursive model beats both the best standard model and an unfactorized standard model on all three evaluations (same data, fewer params, more FLOPs).
claims.evidence_quote: Overall, the recursive models are highly competitive; in the 10M-word setting, our recursive model outperforms both standard models on all three evaluations.

claims.claim: At 100M words, the 404M RecursiveGPT-Large reaches the best average score, above a 1.22B standard model trained on the same data, while the 124M recursive model trails the 1.22B model except on BLiMP.
claims.evidence_quote: Scaling the recursive model to 404.1M parameters yields RecursiveGPT-Large, which uses substantially higher compute and reaches the best average score among our models while still being smaller than the 1.22B standard baseline.

claims.claim: Allocating the recursive model's extra compute to more epochs over the same data instead degrades the standard model, so recursion is a better use of FLOPs when data is the binding constraint.
claims.evidence_quote: Additional epochs reduce the average score from 45.07 to 41.47 at 10M words and from 63.47 to 56.68 at 100M words.

claims.claim: The benefit of recurrent depth is non-monotonic: average score improves up to depth 16 and then declines slightly, attributed to optimization difficulty.
claims.evidence_quote: the average score across the three evaluations improves with recurrent depth up to depth 16 and then declines slightly.

numbers.what: Table 1 parameter counts and BLiMP (Std, Std+FE, Rec R=16 at 10M; Std, Rec R=24, Rec-Large at 100M)
Table 1 LAMBADA p@5 and average scores

numbers.quote: pared with 45.07 for the best standard model from Section 3 and 44.93 for an unfactorized standard model with the same hidden size.
At 10M words, we train for 146 epochs, approximately matching the estimated training FLOPs of RecursiveGPT. At 100M words, we train for 50 epochs.
model sizes from 13M to 1.2B parameters, across two corpora and multiple benchmarks.

limitations: Tiny data regime (10M-100M words); 100M-word recursive models below the identified optimal scale due to compute; fixed recurrence only; FLOP matching for the epoch control is approximate; comparisons to BabyLM winners mix objectives.
survey_notes: Data-constrained regime evidence: when data rather than compute binds, recursion beats both adding parameters (overfits) and adding epochs at roughly matched FLOPs. This reconciles with Iso-Depth (2604.21106), which is data-abundant (FineWeb-Edu, tokens grow with compute) and finds looping loses at matched FLOPs: the sign of the looping effect depends on whether data is limited. Same direction as Ouro's 'data-constrained era' motivation and Parcae's iso-param results. Compare with Looped GPT-BERT (2609.09691) in the same BabyLM setting.

title: Beyond What Seems Necessary: Hidden Gains from Scaling Training-Time Reasoning Length under Outcome Supervision
relevance_reason: Theory plus a synthetic looped-Transformer experiment showing OOD accuracy keeps improving with training-time loop count after ID saturates; the other half is RL token budgets.
one_sentence: Shows theoretically and empirically that under outcome-only supervision OOD performance can keep improving as training-time reasoning length (loop count or RL token budget) grows after ID accuracy saturates; looped single-block Transformers on 4-hop induction gain OOD up to ~44 loops.
key_contributions: Theory: self-iteration strengthens inductive bias and, with regularization, reduces reliance on ID-only shortcuts as iterations grow.
Looped one-block Transformer on p-hop induction (p=4): ID saturates near 100% by ~2 loops while OOD keeps rising up to ~44 loops (robust to loop embeddings, ~36 loops).
Parallel finding for RL token budgets on math: OOD gains continue past the budget where ID saturates.

setup.model_sizes: single Transformer block, d_model 256, 8 heads, MLP 512
setup.train_tokens_or_data: synthetic 4-hop induction sequences (vocab 4, length 12), 20,000 steps, batch 256
setup.loops_train: k in {1,2,4,...,48}, each model trained and evaluated at its k
setup.baselines: same looped model at fewer loops
setup.benchmarks: ID vs OOD validation accuracy on p-hop induction (split by hop-index parity); math RL benchmarks

claims.claim: With parameters and data fixed, increasing training-time loop count keeps improving OOD accuracy long after ID accuracy saturates.
claims.evidence_quote: Increasing the loop count yields OOD gains up to around 44 loops, while ID accuracy saturates near 100% by around 2 loops.

claims.claim: The OOD gains from more loops persist when explicit loop-index embeddings are added, peaking around 36 loops.
claims.evidence_quote: ID accuracy saturates around 2 loops, while OOD accuracy continues improving up to around 36 loops.

claims.claim: Under outcome-only supervision, OOD robustness may require a larger reasoning-length budget than ID validation alone indicates.
claims.evidence_quote: This suggests that robustness may require a larger budget than ID validation alone would indicate.

numbers.quote: To scale latent reasoning depth, the backbone is applied repeatedly for k ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 24, 28, 32, 36, 40, 44, 48} loops, with parameters shared across loops.
We use model dimension 256, with 8 attention heads and MLP hidden dimension 512.
In our experiments, we set p = 4, the vocabulary size to 4, and the sequence length to 12.

limitations: Looped evidence is a single tiny synthetic task; OOD is defined by hop-index parity rather than longer horizons or depth extrapolation; each loop count is trained separately, so no test-time extrapolation is studied.
survey_notes: Supports 'more training-time depth helps generalization beyond what ID metrics show' but only on a synthetic task at iso_param (FLOPs grow with loops). Not evidence about test-time extrapolation beyond the trained horizon. Contrasts with LM-scale findings where loops beyond 2-4 regress under FLOP matching (SMELT 2609.01343, LoopCoder-v2 2606.18023): different regime (iso_param, synthetic, no FLOP matching).

title: Evaluating Tiny Recursive Models Across Training for Code Generation
relevance_reason: Autoregressive Tiny Recursive Model (shared 2-layer block, effective depth 20) for NL-to-Python, compared with iso-parameter and iso-depth Transformer controls across training.
one_sentence: A ~28M TRM-AR (2-layer block reused to effective depth 20) beats an iso-parameter 2-layer Transformer on fit and generated-code quality, but loses to an iso-depth 20-layer Transformer at its validation optimum; its edge is resistance to overfitting, at ~175x per-step cost.
key_contributions: Crossover-curve evaluation of teacher-forced fit vs free-running generation across 40 epochs and 3 seeds with iso-parameter and iso-depth controls.
At equal parameters TRM-AR recovers ~45% of the validation-loss gap and ~57% of the generation-quality gap between the two controls.
At equal effective depth the larger plain Transformer fits and generates better; recursion is parameter-efficient but not compute-efficient.

setup.model_sizes: ~28M parameters; vanilla-2L (iso-param) and vanilla-20L (iso-depth, 1.68x total, ~10x non-embedding params)
setup.loops_train: T=2 cycles of n=4 latent updates plus 1 answer update (effective depth 20), deep supervision over 3 steps, one-step gradient
setup.benchmarks: validation loss, LLM-judge generation quality, AST-parse rate

claims.claim: At equal parameters, TRM-AR fits, generates and generalizes better than a 2-layer Transformer, recovering roughly half of the gap to the 20-layer control.
claims.evidence_quote: At equal parameters, TRM-AR fits, generates, and generalizes better than the parameter-matched control while recovering approximately 45% of the validation-loss gap and 57% of the generation-quality gap between the two controls

claims.claim: At equal effective depth, a 20-layer Transformer with ~10x the non-embedding parameters fits and generates better at its validation optimum; TRM-AR's remaining advantage is resistance to overfitting.
claims.evidence_quote: However, at equal effective depth, the larger transformer fits and generates better at its validation optimum, suggesting TRM-AR’s advantage lies in resistance to overfitting, not greater capability.

claims.claim: Recursion is parameter-efficient but not compute-efficient: per-step time is ~175x the iso-parameter control and ~2.4x the iso-depth control.
claims.evidence_quote: Realizing an effective depth of 20 by looping a two-layer block costs roughly 175× the per-step time of the iso-parameter control and about 2.4× that of the iso-depth control

numbers.quote: at roughly 175× the per-step cost of the parameter-matched control.
vanilla-20L (iso-depth control): twenty independent layers, matching TRM-AR’s effective depth of 20 at 1.68× the total, or ≈ 10× the non-embedding, parameters [37].
TRM-AR realizes an effective depth of 20 by recursively reusing the shared two-layer block (Eq. 1), at essentially the parameter budget of a two-layer model.

limitations: Single small scale (~28M) and one corpus; recursion is entangled with deep supervision and TRM architecture; generation judged by an LLM; one-step gradient approximation.
survey_notes: Clean small-scale regime split: wins at iso_param, loses at iso_effective_depth, matching Iso-Depth (2604.21106) and Ouro App. D. Shows ranking flips across checkpoints, a methodological warning for single-checkpoint claims. Attributes the iso-param advantage to implicit regularization under limited data, consistent with RecursiveGPT (2608.26973).

title: LatentMT: Machine Translation with Latent Reasoning
relevance_reason: LoRA-adapts the Ouro-2.6B-Thinking looped LM for machine translation and studies translation quality versus fixed recurrent depth.
one_sentence: Per-language-pair LoRA on a frozen Ouro-2.6B-Thinking backbone with fixed recurrent depth u gives MT quality comparable to 3-5x larger models over 32 directions; gains come mostly from u=1 to u=2 and saturate quickly.
key_contributions: First systematic study of looped LMs for MT across 32 directions (high, mid, low resource) with swappable LoRA adapters on one frozen looped backbone.
Recurrent-depth sweep with early exit disabled: large gain from u=1 to u=2, then saturation; hidden-state differences shrink across steps.
Same-protocol comparison against Qwen3-8B SFT, plus comparisons to specialized MT systems.

setup.loops_train: fixed u per run (adaptive exit disabled)
setup.baselines: Qwen3-8B with the same SFT protocol; out-of-box Ouro; DRT-14B, ExTrans-7B, Google NMT, EMMA-500-8B (unmatched)

claims.evidence_quote: Across 32 translation directions spanning high-, mid-, and low-resource languages, LatentMT achieves performance comparable to models three to five times larger.

claims.evidence_quote: Most of the gain from additional recurrent computation appears early: moving from u = 1 to u = 2 adds 7.65 BLEU, 9.35 COMET, and 9.86 COMETKiwi

claims.evidence_quote: LatentMT achieves the best overall score among all compared systems, peaking at 24.47 BLEU with u = 4. This is 7.28 BLEU above fine-tuned Google NMT and 5.31 BLEU above Qwen3-8B SFT

Parameter-efficiency claim is unmatched. Translation is closer to knowledge/fluency than multi-step reasoning, so this is weak evidence either way for the 'reasoning not storage' hypothesis.

title: How Model Growth, Recursion, and Boundary Operators Influence Scaling Exponents
relevance_reason: Compute-optimal scaling ladders for prelude-core-coda looped, untied, grown and boundary-operator transformers, measuring exponent vs constant changes and multi-epoch loop scaling.
one_sentence: Fits separate compute-optimal laws (1e18-1e20 FLOPs) per architecture: model growth and a boundary operator (normalize + re-inject prelude) raise the scaling exponent, weight tying costs only a constant factor, and with repeated data the optimal loop count rises with compute.
key_contributions: Prelude-core-coda family isolating boundary operator (Vanilla vs Operator-1), weight sharing (Loop-2 vs Untied-2) and growth (doubling core passes mid-training), each with its own compute-optimal recipe.
Exponent results: Vanilla 0.111, Operator-1/Loop-2/Untied-2 0.114, Loop-Grow 0.116, Untied-Grow 0.117; untying shifts only the constant (1.08x at 1e18, 1.06x at 1e20 over Loop-2).

Multi-epoch (100M unique tokens, 10 epochs): optimal loop count grows from ~1.4 to ~6.7 with compute; loop scaling matches best weight-decay-tuned size scaling with 2.2x less compute. Extrapolated 7.4B Untied-Grow lands on the fitted curve.

setup.model_sizes: compute-optimal ladders d-ell at width/depth 128 (e.g. d8 width 1024); multi-epoch grid 120M-1.4B; extrapolation run 7.4B (starts at 5B)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: FineWeb (single epoch) and FineWeb-Edu; multi-epoch: 100M unique FineWeb tokens x 10 epochs
setup.loops_train: K=2 fixed (Loop-2/Untied-2), K=2 to 4 growth; multi-epoch Loop-1 to Loop-12
setup.baselines: Vanilla pre-norm transformer with its own compute-optimal recipe; Operator-1; Deep Vanilla
setup.benchmarks: FineWeb validation loss; CORE; answer NLL

claims.claim: Architectural changes can alter the compute-optimal scaling exponent: model growth gives the largest gain and a boundary operator alone also raises it, with compute multipliers over Vanilla that grow with scale.
claims.evidence_quote: Growing the model during training, by increasing the number of core passes with untied weights, improves the scaling exponent. The grown model reaches the loss of a standard transformer with 1.55× less compute at 1020 FLOPs, and this gap widens with scale.

claims.claim: At matched FLOPs and executed depth, weight tying (Loop-2) versus untied cores (Untied-2) costs a fixed compute factor that does not grow with scale.
claims.evidence_quote: Weight sharing therefore costs a fixed factor of compute at every scale, rather than a factor that grows with the budget.

claims.claim: Growing the number of tied loops during training keeps Vanilla's parameter count yet gives a 1.36x compute multiplier over a standard transformer at 1e20 FLOPs.
claims.evidence_quote: Growing the number of loops with tied weights obtains the exponent improvement from growth with the same number of parameters as a vanilla transformer, and trails untied growth by only a small constant factor, for a 1.36× compute multiplier over a standard transformer at 1020 FLOPs.

claims.claim: With repeated data, looping regularizes: the optimal loop count grows with compute and loop scaling beats weight-decay-tuned model-size scaling by 2.2x compute; untied looping does not beat tuned Operator-1.
claims.evidence_quote: Scaling the loop count at fixed model size and fixed weight decay matches that loss with 2.2× less compute, and tuning weight decay on top gains at most 0.02, so loop-count scaling is more compute-efficient and nearly free of tuning.

claims.claim: A 7.4B Untied-Grow model matches the estimated GPT-3 13B CORE score with about 20x less compute; the authors flag this as indicative only (different data and evaluation).
claims.evidence_quote: The two models were trained on different data, and the GPT-3 reference is an estimate from a separate evaluation pipeline, so the roughly 20× gap is indicative rather than a controlled comparison.

numbers.value: Vanilla 0.111; Operator-1 0.114; Loop-2 0.114; Untied-2 0.114; Loop-Grow 0.116; Untied-Grow 0.117
numbers.quote: Vanilla (γ = 0.111) Operator-1 (γ = 0.114) Loop-2 (γ = 0.114) Untied-2 (γ = 0.114) Loop-Grow (γ = 0.116) Untied-Grow (γ = 0.117)

Untied-2 is 1.08× above Loop-2 at 1018 FLOPs and 1.06× at 1020 , and Untied-Grow is 1.16× and 1.14× above Loop-Grow at the same budgets.
its multiplier over Vanilla increases with scale, from 1.12× at 1018 FLOPs to 1.25× at 1020 FLOPs.
The 7.4B Untied-Grow model reaches 0.3865 CORE, on par with the GPT-3 13B reference of 0.3852 (Karpathy, a), at 1.23 × 1021 FLOPs against 2.31 × 1022 for GPT-3 13B

limitations: Exponent differences are small (0.111 vs 0.117) and fitted over two decades of compute; the headline 7.4B model is untied growth, not weight-tied looping; GPT-3 comparison is unmatched; looping benefits in the single-epoch regime are mixed with the boundary operator.
survey_notes: Adds three nuances to the scaling section: (1) the cost of weight tying at matched FLOPs and executed depth is a constant factor (~1.06-1.08x) rather than growing with scale, softer than Iso-Depth's phi=0.46 framing (2604.21106) but in the same direction; the two differ in matching (here each arm has its own compute-optimal width/tokens). (2) The input-injection/normalization 'boundary operator' used by looped designs is itself a source of gains even without looping, so looped-vs-vanilla comparisons that add injection confound the two. (3) In the data-constrained multi-epoch regime, looping is a better use of compute than more parameters, agreeing with RecursiveGPT (2608.26973) and Parcae's iso-param story (2604.12946).

title: Beyond Parameters: Exploring Virtual Logic Depth for Scaling Laws
relevance_reason: Controlled layer-reuse (sequence, cycle, inverse-cycle) study separating knowledge capacity from reasoning at fixed parameters.
one_sentence: Repeating tied layers (virtual logical depth) leaves measured knowledge capacity nearly unchanged at fixed parameters but raises synthetic iGSM math accuracy, e.g. a 4-layer model from 46.3% to 70.7% with cycle factor 5.
key_contributions: Knowledge capacity measured by information absorbed from random-token sequences (GPT-2, 5M-20M): constant across VLD patterns and factors, scaling only with parameters.
Reasoning on iGSM (trained from scratch, 50M-200M): VLD improves accuracy; a 50M cycle model at effective depth 12 edges out a native 150M 12-layer model.
LoRA SFT of Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct with cycle VLD reports gains on Math500, AIME, GPQA, HumanEval, MBPP.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: 640K random tokens (capacity); 500K iGSM problems with <=15 operations; 2.3B-token SFT corpus
setup.baselines: same base model without reuse; deeper native models (iso-effective-depth with more params)
setup.benchmarks: absorbed bits; iGSM op15/op20/op21 accuracy; Math500, AIME, GPQA, HumanEval, MBPP

claims.claim: At fixed parameters, adding virtual depth through layer reuse leaves knowledge capacity nearly unchanged, while capacity scales with parameter count across models.
claims.evidence_quote: At a fixed parameter count, VLD leaves knowledge capacity nearly unchanged (with only minor variance), while across models knowledge capacity scales with the number of parameters

claims.claim: Layer reuse substantially improves synthetic multi-step math reasoning at fixed parameters.
claims.evidence_quote: the cycle pattern achieves substantial improvements, increasing the 4-layer model’s accuracy from 46.3% to 70.7% with a VLD factor of 5.

claims.claim: At equal effective depth (12), a 50M looped model slightly exceeds a native 150M 12-layer model on iGSM op15.
claims.evidence_quote: For instance, the 50M-parameter model using the cycle pattern (factor 2, effective depth=12) achieves 62.05% accuracy, surpassing the native 150Mparameter model (12-layer)

claims.claim: Scaling with VLD is non-monotonic in places (factor 3 below factor 2; depth 32 below depth 16).
claims.evidence_quote: cycle pattern shows VLD factor 3 (61.6%) performing slightly worse than factor 2 (62.1%) for the 4-layer model, and Figure 3(c) shows depth 32 yielding lower accuracy than depth 16.

numbers.quote: increasing the 4-layer model’s accuracy from 46.3% to 70.7% with a VLD factor of 5.
We established four 4-layer GPT-2 models with increasing parameter counts (5M, 10M, 15M, and 20M).
we designed experiments to store approximately 10M bits of information (aligning with the 2 bits per parameter capacity), requiring a sequence length of approximately k = 640,000 random tokens.

limitations: Small synthetic models; real-world evidence is a LoRA SFT of one 3B model with layer repetition; single seeds (multi-seed statistics deferred); repetition adds FLOPs, so not compute-matched.
venue: Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2026
survey_notes: Independent confirmation of Ouro's storage-vs-manipulation split (2510.25741) using a different capacity measure (random tokens) at iso_param. Its iso-effective-depth win on synthetic iGSM aligns with Saunshi-style reasoning results but contrasts with LM-loss studies at iso-effective-depth (Iso-Depth 2604.21106, Ouro App. D, TRM-AR 2608.29376) where unique layers win; the task (synthetic reasoning vs general LM/knowledge) explains the difference.

title: Scaling Laws vs Model Architectures: How does Inductive Bias Influence Scaling?
relevance_reason: Ten-architecture scaling comparison in T5 seq2seq that includes Universal Transformers and ALBERT (weight-shared depth) among other variants.
one_sentence: Scales ten T5-style architectures on C4 and finds weight-shared models scale poorly: UT is among the hardest to scale, ALBERT trends negatively, and adding UT recurrent operations does not improve performance despite more FLOPs.
key_contributions: Systematic upstream/downstream scaling slopes for ten architectures including Universal Transformer and seq2seq ALBERT.
Finding that best architecture changes with scale and that upstream perplexity scaling need not transfer downstream.
Negative early evidence on scaling recurrence: more UT recurrences did not help even with more FLOPs.

setup.model_sizes: tiny to XL-scale T5-style models (up to ~2.1e9 parameters on plot axes; UT scaled via d_ff up to 32K and recurrences NR1-NR6)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: C4 English pretraining, 2^19 steps; finetuning on GLUE/SuperGLUE/SQuAD mixture
setup.baselines: vanilla Transformer and eight other architectures

claims.claim: Universal Transformers are among the architectures that are difficult to scale, especially downstream, compared with the vanilla Transformer.
claims.evidence_quote: there are models which are difficult to scale such as LConv, UT, MLP-Mixer and Performer. This is even more evident on downstream task.

claims.claim: Increasing the number of UT recurrent operations did not improve performance even though it increased FLOPs.
claims.evidence_quote: Initially we tried scaling the number of recurrent operations. However, we found that even with an increase of FLOPS, this does not lead to improved performance.

claims.claim: Seq2seq ALBERT (parameters shared across all layers and encoder/decoder) scales negatively as model size grows.
claims.evidence_quote: We also note that ALBERT scales (trends) negatively2 (gets worse) as we scale the model up.

numbers.quote: For fair comparison, all models are pretrained for 219 steps on the english C4 corpus optimized using an inverse square root learning rate

limitations: Pre-2023 recipes (no input injection, no stability fixes); encoder-decoder T5 setting; UT scaling explored only coarsely; architectures not FLOP-matched.
survey_notes: Historical baseline for the scaling section: early evidence that naive weight-shared depth (UT, ALBERT) scales worse than unique layers, and that adding recurrences at fixed parameters did not help in T5 pretraining. Later work (Huginn, Parcae 2604.12946) attributes such failures partly to instability fixed by input injection and spectral constraints; Iso-Depth (2604.21106) still finds a sharing cost at matched FLOPs.

title: Looped GPT-BERT: Trading Parameters for Computation in Small Language Modeling
relevance_reason: Depth-wise weight-shared small LM (4 physical layers x 12 traversals) in the BabyLM 2026 Strict-small setting with loop-count ablations.
one_sentence: A 12.18M-parameter GPT-BERT with four physical layers looped 12 times (input re-injected each loop) trained on 7.48M words gives BabyLM Strict-small performance comparable to larger public baselines on selected metrics, with diminishing returns from more loops.
key_contributions: Combines GPT-BERT's masked-next-token/causal objectives with depth-wise recurrent parameter sharing.
Compares a 12-layer non-looped model with 4 physical layers applied 1/3/6/12 times.
BabyLM 2026 leaderboard entry with released checkpoints.

setup.baselines: 12-layer non-looped model; public BabyLM 10M Strict-small GPT-2 and GPT-BERT baselines
setup.benchmarks: BLiMP, BLiMP Supplement, EWoK, Entity Tracking, COMPS, GlobalPIQA, GLUE/SuperGLUE subset, Reading, AoA

claims.claim: With far fewer parameters, the looped model is comparable to public BabyLM Strict-small baselines on selected linguistic and downstream metrics (baselines differ in size and recipe).
claims.regime: unmatched (same BabyLM data budget, different models)
claims.evidence_quote: Compared with public BabyLM 10M Strict-small GPT-2 and GPT-BERT baselines, it achieves comparable performance on selected linguistic and downstream metrics, including BLiMP and GLUE, with fewer parameters.

claims.claim: More loops help training and preserve linguistic performance, but weaker results on other tasks suggest few physical layers restrict representational space.
claims.evidence_quote: whereas poorer performance on other tasks may reveal an inherent limitation of the looped design: using only a few physical layers restricts the model's representational space.
